title: Echo Flight incident

tellings.link_reason: Both are about the 1967 Echo Flight missile shutdown at Malmstrom.

tellings.quote: On March 16, 1967, ten Minuteman-I nuclear missiles operated by Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana, suddenly malfunctioned one after the other, just as a “large round object” was reported to be hovering “directly over” one of them—according to retired USAF Col. Walter Figel, one of two launch officers on duty at Echo Flight during the incident.

Figel received the startling news while in the flight's underground launch control center, via a two-way radio call from an Air Force security guard posted at the missile silo in question. Although skeptical, then-Lt. Figel dispatched a couple of two-man Security Alert Teams to the field to investigate. They subsequently confirmed the presence of the UFO.

In an earlier conversation with me, Carlson himself claimed to have no recollection of a UFO report during the full-flight missile shutdown and further claimed that he recalled no mention of UFOs during the debriefing.

plain: On 16 March 1967, ten nuclear missiles at Echo Flight, a group of silos run from Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, are said to have failed one after another while a UFO hovered over one of them. That would mean something unknown could switch off American nuclear weapons. A former Air Force officer named Robert Salas passes on what the launch officer Walter Figel told him: at first Figel could not believe the guards' report, 'but very shortly after that, all 10 of his missiles went down.' Michels places the case eight days before Salas's own incident and ties it to later cases at Malmstrom. In a 2012 article the researcher Robert Hastings writes, on Figel's word, that a 'large round object' was reported hovering 'directly over' a silo and that security teams sent out 'confirmed the presence of the UFO'. Hastings also records that the missile commander, Eric Carlson, 'claimed to have no recollection of a UFO report', a claim Hastings disputes but keeps, while the spoken tellings leave it out.

discussion.by: The Echo and Oscar Flight Incidents
discussion.text: Hastings writes that ten missiles "suddenly malfunctioned one after the other, just as a “large round object” was reported to be hovering “directly over” one of them", on the word of the deputy launch officer, Walter Figel; he also records that the missile commander, Eric Carlson, "claimed to have no recollection of a UFO report during the full-flight missile shutdown", a claim Hastings disputes. The tellers give the UFO report without the commander's dissent, which the article keeps.
